ateret-zekenim/3:_: However one must see that there is not so much [impurity] etc. My teacher ruled that mouse-bitten [grain] is not [forbidden] on account of chametz, as Rashba [holds], and also flour in flour mixes well — not as Maharam Isserles wrote that sprouted grain must be baked before Pesach, for that is not so. And his words contradict what he wrote in siman 464 that flour is like dough in dough; nevertheless every person of spirit should be concerned for himself, especially regarding sprouted grain, and one must guard the flour from the time of grinding until after baking — at least so [writes] Rashi in Chullin daf 7a; see there.
ateret-zekenim/6:_: One must untie [the stitching] etc. And some say that even if there is no stitching or patches one should not place Pesach flour in them — such is the practice — and not as Shulchan Aruch writes here and in siman 451 to untie [stitching].
biur-halacha/1:_: And some forbid — see in Mishna Berurah the reason. And we copied here the words of our teacher Menachem in his commentary to Rambam: after he brought several weak reasons for this custom he concludes thus: Afterwards I found written that there is one species called witzash and they are groats of wheat that change in their land in form and nature like zunin; and in a year that is not blessed the crop goes out of the normal way and returns zunin from the language "the land played the harlot"; and in a rainy year the crop returns witzash and they call it witzash parmantelsh — therefore they forbade all kitniyot, end quote there. And the explanation of his words is that there are types of wheat that in a year that is not as it should be change and appear like types of seeds — therefore they forbade all types of seeds.
biur-halacha/3:_: If they did not separate the wheat etc. — from this language it implies l'chatchila one must separate those bitten by mice; but in Tur and likewise in Levush it is found that one need not even l'chatchila; and so in Ma'amar Mordechai; and it is possible the Mechaber deals when there is not sixty against them, and therefore it is fit l'chatchila to separate them [Peri Megadim].
biur-halacha/4:א: Good to guard them etc. from the time of harvest — and the Peri Chadash decides that guarding from harvest is by law and for ab initio and even b'dieved; and so his words are found in several Rishonim that guarding is from harvest; and even if one does not find matzah guarded from harvest for the sake of matzah, we can certainly rely on Shulchan Aruch and recite the blessing of eating matzah; nevertheless l'chatchila it is certainly correct to be stringent for matzah of the mitzvah to take specifically matzah guarded from harvest; and in the name of the Gra they also brought that he was very stringent not to eat except what is guarded from harvest, and he was careful in this all the days of Pesach — from concern lest water fell on them while attached after the grain dried.
biur-halacha/4:ב: (ב) And at least one hour of grinding, and if it is permissible to send flour that is kept on the entrance without the Israeli guard, see the book of Jerusalem extensions, which is not determined to send without a guard, and to the rainfall of the rainforests from the Temple Mount, and the psalmist said: "This is a sign that you should not be sent without a guard, and it is a sign that is a sign."
biur-halacha/4:ג: (ג) And at the time of the press and so on from the market, see the U.S. and even at the time of the better pressure to take flour from a scoon or of planting foxes from the market because it is to give it and it should not be given
biur-halacha/4:ד: From the marketplace — from the conclusion of the wording it implies that even from a non-Jew it is permitted, for we do not establish a prohibition unless one must pick them initially lest there be crumbs of chametz, as explained in Shibolei Leket siman 200 in the name of Rashi, and so explicitly in several Rishonim. However in Chiddushei Ritva to Pesachim he is very stringent here and thus: It is reasonable that their flour is forbidden on Pesach, for through grinding in water-millstones it is common for water to rise in them; and so is the view of Ra'ah; and even flour of Israel left from the rest of the year that was not guarded properly — he doubts there. Nevertheless at the end he concludes: and in flour of Israel we do not forbid b'dieved, but of a non-Jew it is forbidden, for that one certainly leaves them in a ruinous place as he can, and his teachers agreed that even in a time of duress one does not permit them at all. And the Geonim wrote that it is permitted to take flour from the marketplace in time of duress and we do not establish prohibition, and one fulfills his obligation thereby. And he wrote on this: wherever one has no other flour in any way at all, one makes matzah from flour of a non-Jew and eats from it an olive-bulk for the mitzvah, for this concern is [only] a rabbinic issur of something [forbidden in] mixture; and in a place of the Torah mitzvah of matzah we are not concerned — even though a court may stipulate to uproot something from the Torah in shev v'al ta'aseh, that is only where there is a definite prohibition; but here the concern is remote and it is possible there is no prohibition, end quote. And from other Rishonim it implies we are not stringent b'dieved, and even all the days of Pesach it is permitted; see Bach.
chatam-sofer/1:_: In Magen Avraham note 1 — to become chametz, Turkish [grain] — see responsa Chatam Sofer OC siman 50 and siman 121 regarding wheat of Togarma.
chatam-sofer/2:_: (This is the name of Section A. in The Hague) and the custom in Ashkenazi, and see the answers of the C.C., [about the leaders of his country and the nebula who have been allowed to eat mini-cataine in the midst of Passover and hastened to speak well:
chatam-sofer/3:_: Those [grains] on the water — see below siman 467 seif 3; and in any case Radbaz in responsa part 1, second [volume] siman 286 wrote: one who guards his soul should distance himself, because when the measure is lacking the sailors pour water to fill their lack; and in any case it appears to me that one should not take from them matzah for the mitzvah, for it requires guarding le-shemah from when it approaches the water, for it is no less than water-millstones; and so I taught the practical halacha in Chatam Sofer OC siman 134; and see in Magen Avraham siman 466 note 9; and see below siman 467 seif 6 what is written on the margin.
chokhmat-shlomo/1:_: Seif 1: But not in rice etc. — It would seem by law to permit kitniyot on Pesach in time of duress, as we wrote in our works several times debating whether one can apply "a court cannot annul [the enactment] of its fellow court." Now God enlightened my eyes and I found further permission from the Gemara Pesachim chapter 1 daf 3b: R' Zeira said to R' Elazar (and some say R' Eliezer to R' Yehoshua): R' Gamliel and the court — how can they annul the enactment of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel? Did we not learn: a court cannot annul the enactment of its fellow court unless it is greater in wisdom and number? He was astonished one hour. He said to him: say they stipulated among themselves that whoever wishes to annul may come and annul etc. From this it is clear that only where we know they did not so stipulate may a court not annul its fellow's enactment; but without such knowledge one may hang that perhaps they stipulated they could annul; and it is permitted to annul — and this is since it is only a rabbinic enactment, it is a rabbinic doubt, and we are lenient. Thus the language "say they so enacted" implies doubt, and on account of doubt they were lenient — not that R' Gamliel and the court knew they enacted for this; for then it would not say "say," since it is known R' Gamliel and the court annulled the enactment perforce knowing they so stipulated — then it should say "they stipulated among themselves" or "they knew they so stipulated"; and from saying "say" it is proven they too had doubt and permitted on account of doubt. And what the Gemara challenges in Megillah "a court cannot annul" and does not answer "say they stipulated" — that is because there it is words of tradition like Torah law, a doubt for stringency. And what it challenges in Gittin regarding prozbul — there it is a presumption of obligation, the borrower was certainly liable, and a doubt whether he was released by shemittah or not, like "I do not know if I paid you" — liable; therefore it challenges well they could not annul prozbul and release the borrower. And what it challenges in Avodah Zarah daf 36 regarding oil — although there it is only rabbinic, there it challenges two difficulties: first, a court cannot annul; then Rav Huna said in the name of R' Yochanan: in everything a court may annul its fellow's enactment except eighteen matters etc. — and it is astonishing how R' Yochanan can disagree with the Mishnah; behold an anonymous [Mishnah] implies in every matter a court cannot annul etc. But per the above, the Mishnah is specifically where it is known they did not stipulate initially that whoever wishes may annul; then in no matter may a court annul; but R' Yochanan deals with doubt whether they stipulated, and R' Yochanan according to his method in Pesachim answers "say they stipulated"; or even per the girsa there R' Avahu — nevertheless R' Yochanan may hold so, and therefore in doubt whether they stipulated initially, he holds in every matter a court may annul except eighteen matters; even in doubt one may not annul. Thus it fits: initially before knowing R' Yochanan's words it seemed truly even in doubt one cannot annul; but after bringing R' Yochanan's words one knows even in doubt one may annul, only it challenges regarding oil which was among the eighteen matters. And the upshot: where there is doubt whether they stipulated, they may annul a fellow court's enactment — all the more so in later enactments; and one should not be stringent. So it appears to me; and see in my work on YD laws of tereifot siman 33 edition 6 siman 207 what I wrote incidentally related to this law — see there and examine well.
chokhmat-shlomo/2:_: (There, seif 3 in the gloss) And similarly if they did not separate sprouted grain — however one must see it is not so much that there is not sixty against it from the permitted. It appears by law: if there is not sixty in the wheat against the sprouts, whether it is permitted to add another species such as buckwheat etc. — it appears forbidden; not only to fulfill matzah obligation — certainly forbidden; one: concern for those who hold even in such a mixture one does not fulfill matzah except with rice, not other species; two: even for those who permit other species, perhaps combined with buckwheat there will not be an olive-bulk within the time of eating a meal from the permitted species for matzah alone; three: even for those who hold taste suffices, that is when the taste is only from what is permitted on Pesach — then since taste is sensed it is as if in essence; but here there are sprouts too, also a grain species — in the sprouts one does not fulfill matzah by taste; and from taste there is no proof it is as if in essence, lest it be in combination with sprouts; therefore certainly one does not fulfill; only for permitted eating it does not appear so. Bach is brought in Magen Avraham end siman 447: forbidden to mix even before Pesach to eat on Pesach; so implies Tzemach Tzedek whom Magen Avraham brought; even Magen Avraham who disagrees only because he does not intend to mix to eat on Pesach — if he mixed to eat on Pesach he would concede forbidden; so Mishnah Berurah siman 442 notes 18, 14; and Tur brought there; even per Taz who permits siman 447 — examination is needed. I answer: in Shulchan Aruch Shabbat siman 254 seif 4 he wrote: even if one put a little oil etc. one may not light with them — see Taz and Magen Avraham: reason — we decree lest one come to light in essence; however one could say specifically if he put a little oil in his hands intentionally to permit lighting — that is forbidden by this decree since he does so intentionally; but if it mixed by itself without intent we do not decree; and truly l'chatchila one does not nullify prohibition; and one could say from that reason itself we decree lest one eat in essence; yet this is difficult: why for a rabbinic prohibition may one add and nullify per Mechaber, and why not decree lest one eat in essence — in oil too it is rabbinic and we decree lest one eat in essence; it would seem there it deals when only a little of permitted was put and forbidden was majority — therefore we decree lest one light in essence; so Pri Megadim Shabbat laws wrote; but one who examines the Gemara proves the opposite — if so the Gemara should challenge from Rabbenu Gershom etc.; also more clear from Tosafot there s.v. simchat: it is different, since of permitted there is only a quarter, nullified among other species, as if no flax at all — thus explicitly where there is little permitted one need not decree lest one light in essence, only otherwise forbidden even in the Temple though there this decree does not apply; thus the Gemara's question "what if one puts any amount of oil" — the reason is the decree; yet by law it is forbidden otherwise since oil is little and perforce only Abaye was doubtful perhaps even any amount is as if in essence; but Rabbah who said the reason "one does not light" perforce forbids even much; therefore the reason was needed that for any amount otherwise it would be forbidden by law, especially poskim who gave reason lest one light in essence — how do they disagree with the Gemara's anonymous [view] that any amount is as if no permitted at all? Perforce it deals with majority — and from Tosafot it would be proof for R' Chaim Kohen that minority permitted in majority forbidden joins forbidden to permitted and one is lashed — see there and examine; poskim disagree. From my words it appears: even in majority we decree lest one light in essence — why permit adding to rabbinic prohibition? One must distinguish: there it is rabbinic without a Torah strand, no Torah-prohibition concern — therefore we do not decree a decree on a decree; but in Shabbat laws, since there is a Torah strand lest one tilt to violation, we decree decree on decree; or distinguish: adding a species one sometimes mixes without intent to nullify — we do not decree lest one use in essence; but in oil one mixes other oil not of its kind — no way to mix them, recognizable he does so only to nullify prohibition — we decree lest he use alone. Thus here chametz on Pesach is Torah-forbidden in less than sixty — Taz permits mixing in time of permission, adding its own kind, not recognizable intent to nullify to cancel, for often one mixes wheat with wheat; but if he mixes what is not customary to mix, intent is only to nullify — certainly forbidden; and what helps from time of permission if we fear use in essence, and here Torah prohibition if used without sixty nullification — in Shabbat too mixture and lighting were in time of permission, yet chametz is worse, some say its name clings and it is always in prohibition, but oil was certainly on erev Shabbat in time of permission and we decreed — all the more here; therefore it appears forbidden to add another species — Taz would agree forbidden to mix, especially most forbid nullifying before Pesach intending to eat, as stated; examine well. Regarding onions found in wheat: in my Pesach laws I wrote to permit in sixty relying on Peri Chadash — see there; only in duress, not otherwise. Now I saw even without duress if they are so little that in a thousand they are nullified for all — one may say permitted: combine Rashba brought in Beit Yosef siman 100: bran is nullified in 960 — we see nullification near a thousand even what is not nullified in sixty; even disputants explain Yerushalmi deals with taste — thus taste not nullified in sixty is nullified in 960; so here even if we say fruit juice does not help in sixty, in a thousand it is nullified, as in bran: since not explicit it is not nullified even in a thousand per Rashba, only in sixty — so one may say for a sharp item, especially onions not clearly sharp or fruit juice; so it appears to be lenient; examine well.
dagul-merevavah/1:_: This is not explained in Maharil; and perhaps since the rabbi Maharil was so stringent regarding other oils, he was stringent regarding olive oil as well lest one come to exchange it. However according to Darkei Moshe it is certain one should not decree olive oil because of other oils; nevertheless I have not seen the custom to eat olive oil on Pesach. And further it appears to me a stringency in olive oil: olives are crushed in a mortar as stated in Menachot daf 86a in the Mishnah and Gemara, and olives are called a sharp item — see above siman 447 seif 8 and see siman 451 seif 16 regarding the mortar; therefore one should be concerned lest they were crushed in a mortar in which chametz was crushed. And Darkei Moshe regarding other oils did not be concerned about absorbing taste from the mortar, because other oils are not made from a sharp item; but olive is sharp — if so the matter is reversed and olive oil is worse than other oils; and even b'dieved it appears to me we do not forbid a mixture, but l'chatchila it is forbidden to put olive oil into a cooked dish.
eliyah-rabbah/1:_: (a) a glass. This means atotal walnut that the Aboriginal Kuin drew a carin or rocky
eliyah-rabbah/2:_: But not in rice etc. They call it reyz or hirez and titraki or heydin — so it implies in Yoreh Deah siman 84 and above siman 168; but groifen are forbidden to keep, for they are made from barley and placed in water to remove their shells, and that is moistening in seif 5; and I heard that my ancestor the Gaon zikhrono le-verachah permitted one who forgot and had groifen to sell them to a non-Jew; and it appears astonishing; and it is possible that by law of the Gemara moistening is permitted b'dieved even in barley, as long as it did not split, as Tur wrote siman 467 seif 5; and see Magen Avraham there who wrote that even if it rests calmly it is only a doubt of chametz — see note 9. Chok Yaakov wrote: I heard what they call in this country tyrchin and weitz — it is a type of kitniyot.
eliyah-rabbah/3:_: Who is driving and so on? And don’t a man say that there is no prohibition against a theory, no one can feel any of the grains that pass on him must die, and he goes on and so on
eliyah-rabbah/4:_: If it fell etc. — specifically in a majority of permitted; and see siman 467. In oils etc. — even if they were crushed in a mortar in which barley is soaked — for only regarding a sharp item do we say that under duress it absorbs.
eliyah-rabbah/5:_: They are allowed to stay and so on. Even water fell upon them, and he was the judge to enjoy them:
eliyah-rabbah/6:_: And anise etc. — and they require examination that there not be in them one of the five species; Taz wrote: peled kimmel is permitted, krems kimmel is forbidden, for its seeds resemble grain; and Chok Yaakov permits all of them.
eliyah-rabbah/7:_: [Levush] And its majority etc. — and so he wrote in Shulchan Aruch YD siman 324 seif 9; and since he did not write more stringency — even if there is not an olive-bulk within the time of eating a meal — it implies he holds like Rashba and Raavad that we require an olive-bulk within the time of eating a meal; however it is possible to push in duress; and in Eliyahu Zuta I wrote that so it implies in Beit Yosef, and that is because Rashba agreed to Raavad; and this too appears to me the intent of Magen Avraham; and accordingly in other species we require a majority of grain. And Chok Yaakov ruled like Ramban that in rice, even if there is not an olive-bulk within the time of eating a meal, it suffices; and in Shach to Yoreh Deah there it implies he ruled so in all species; and so implies Rabbenu Yerucham page 42 in the name of the Rosh, because taste is like the essence d'oraisa; nevertheless regarding fulfilling the mitzvah it is certainly fit to be stringent; and in challah it is also a stringency.
eliyah-rabbah/8:_: [Levush] And specifically rice etc. — it implies rice with all five species fulfills as taste of grain; and examination is needed, for in Beit Yosef in the name of Ramban it implies specifically wheat in rice; and so implies Levush YD there. Also it is astonishing to me, for Rabbenu Yerucham page 42 wrote in his name: wheat and barley one rubs to come to matzah and chametz; the species mixed with them — but not spelt, oats, and rye — until here; behold explicitly there is no distinction between rice and other species, only between wheat and barley and between spelt, oats, and rye.
eliyah-rabbah/9:_: [Levush] Hard wheat etc. — therefore even if there is not sixty against them it is permitted b'dieved; and it is possible that specifically wheat, but barley quickly becomes chametz — see seif 5 (Magen Avraham); and in my humble opinion it is not specifically wheat that he said, for we do not find in the Gemara daf 40 a distinction between wheat and barley, only regarding moistening l'chatchila; but b'dieved there is no distinction, and in both they are permitted b'dieved as long as they did not split; and so is explained explicitly in responsum of Ramban siman 150 and responsum of Rashba 428 that he permits because we see they do not split — if so perforce barley too is permitted; and on the contrary we find a reason in the Gemara that wheat is inferior since it is not smooth like barley; and for this reason many poskim forbade wheat even if it did not split, as Beit Yosef wrote siman 467. Also it appears to me what the poskim wrote "hard wheat" means more than flour or dough, as Tur wrote explicitly siman 467 regarding wheat in dough.
eshel-avraham/1:א: (א) Trapped. If he does not have his favorite:
eshel-avraham/1:ב: To become chametz — and he wrote in responsum YD siman 16: fresh beans are perhaps permitted on Pesach from that which we hold one who vows [to abstain] from vegetables is forbidden in fresh beans; if so, specifically old ones are considered grain.
eshel-avraham/1:ג: (ג) And it is not to be changed to this substance that is a bit of evidence from the S. D.D., but that we have not completed our practice as an A. in the same way that we have a nuclei:
eshel-avraham/1:ד: (ד) allowed to stay. But not the kind of rashes as the salts came in the water:
eshel-avraham/4:_: A few hours. There is no difference between the smell and the snares of Dafi because of the wind and the likeness it must be felt:
eshel-avraham/6:_: They require — and likewise matzot: one should not make them on cloths that one placed flour on; Bach permitted the stitching in laundering; and better on a smooth table — Taz and Peri Chadash; and so Maharil warned not to eat on Pesach on a cloth placed on a sack of flour.
eshel-avraham/8:_: The snails in the palm of the stone and honor him beautifully that he will not remain of flour all year. A year later, found in the dance of small, dry furs and were knocked on a white dirt salad. And he looked at him, and his knee was chased as another map that he had been suffocated, but there was no olive in order for him to see him as a burgeon, and that he had no food for him
kaf-hachayyim/1:_: (1) [Seif 1] These are the things through which etc. — on account of the obligation of matzah on the first night, for he is obligated to eat matzah as written "in the evening you shall eat matzot." Rashi Pesachim 35a; and see below siman 475 seif 7 and in our words there b'siyata di-shmaya.
kaf-hachayyim/2:_: (2) There. In wheat and barley etc. — as the verse says: you shall not eat upon it chametz, seven days you shall eat upon it matzot — things that come to chametz, a person fulfills his obligation of matzah with them; rice and millet are excluded, for they do not come to chametz but only to spoilage. Gemara there; and Rashi explained: rice and millet do not make chametz, and if one makes them chametz they spoil — end quote; and so Levush; and see below orot 7.
kaf-hachayyim/3:_: (3) There. In wheat and barley and spelt etc. — spelt is a type of wheat; oats (shibbolet shu'al) — its stalk is made like a fox's tail (Rashi in the Mishnah there); rye is a type of barley — Gemara there.
kaf-hachayyim/4:_: (4) There. In wheat and barley etc. — he listed wheat first because it is earlier in the verse "a land of wheat and barley" etc.; and he listed barley before spelt although it is a type of wheat, because barley is of the seven species and therefore precedes spelt, as written above siman 168 seif 4; and he preceded spelt to oats and rye because spelt is a type of wheat. However in the Mishnah there rye precedes oats; and so above siman 168 orot 19 that rye precedes oats — see there; and see in orot afterward.
kaf-hachayyim/5:_: (5) There, gloss. And the custom to take wheat l'chatchila — for it is the best and earliest for the mitzvah — Levush. And if he has no wheat, Kaf HaChayyim wrote orot 2 that here according to all, the species beloved to him comes first in order to fulfill more mitzvot of eating matzah with appetite — see there; and so Chayei Adam orot 1, 2; however if all are equal to him in belovedness, then he takes in the order we wrote in the previous orot.
kaf-hachayyim/6:_: (6) There. But not in rice — and that is what they call reyz or hirez, and likewise tartari they call heydin — responsum Maharam of Lublin siman 78; Kaf HaChayyim orot 3, 2; and I heard that what they call in these countries (Ashkenazic cities) tyrchin and weitz are not included in wheat at all, but are considered kitniyot species — Kaf HaChayyim orot 1, Rama there; 1:1, 1:2; R' Zeira orot 3.
kaf-hachayyim/7:_: (7) There. And also they do not come to chametz — and even if one kneaded rice flour and the like while hot and covered it in garments until it swelled like dough that became chametz — Rashi permits eating it, for this is not chametz but spoilage; Rambam chapter 5 law 1, and so Kol Bo siman 48; Rashi orot 1; and so from words of Tur and Shulchan Aruch who wrote "and also they do not come to chametz" — it implies they do not come to chametz at all in any manner; and so from what is written above orot 2 in the name of Rashi and Levush; and so from words of Rivash 135 ch. 3 who wrote: and it is permitted to make from them every type of cooked dish — see there. And what is written there in Rambam — Raavad's hasagot: this matter is not simple and not all agree to it etc. — that is on law 2, if one kneaded in fruit juice; and as Mishnah Berurah wrote there, that he copied it in law 2; and so Yere'im in Hagahot; and so from words of our master, as he did not speak at all on Raavad's hasagot mentioned, because he relied on Mishnah Berurah; and also because it is true that not all agree regarding kneading in fruit juice, as Tur and Beit Yosef wrote siman 462 — see there; see Kaf HaChayyim orot 4.
kaf-hachayyim/8:_: (8) There. And it is permitted to make from them a cooked dish — Rabbenu Yerucham: one should not eat rice after its prohibition spread in several communities; the rabbi Mahari Zayin in responsa Shaarei Yeshuah part 1, gate 6 siman 4; and so practiced whole [communities] and so many; Birkei Yosef orot 1; and see below orot 10.
kaf-hachayyim/9:_: (9) There, gloss. And some forbid — so too in Hagahot Maimoniot chapter 5 in the name of Semak: kitniyot such as beans and lentils — some practice prohibition not to eat them on Pesach; and so Rabbi Shmuel of Ivria; but Rabbi Yechiel and other great ones practiced leniency with them; and the matter is very difficult to permit, since others practiced prohibition with them. And it appears they did not practice prohibition on account of chametz, for people do not err in this, for schoolchildren know it, for in Peirush we say in the Gemara it does not come to chametz but only the five species; rather they are forbidden because grain is a cooked-dish item and kitniyot are a cooked-dish item — a decree lest one be confused with the other; and also there are places that make bread from kitniyot and one comes to confuse it with dough that is a cooked-dish item; but types of vegetables that are not similar to grain at all do not come to be confused; and also sometimes grain is mixed in them and it is impossible to separate well; and mustard likewise some forbid on Pesach because it is considered grain, even though in their days it was permitted; nevertheless now one should be stringent in these generations who are not so expert in prohibition and permission as the early generations, as Rav Saadiah Gaon explained, end quote; and so Mordechai chapter Kol Sha'ah 27 in the name of Semak; and Bach and Beit Yosef wrote: none are concerned for these words except Ashkenazim; and so Darkei Moshe orot 2: and we Ashkenazim practice stringency; and such are his words here in gloss to Shulchan Aruch: and the custom in Ashkenaz is to be stringent and one should not change; and so Levush; and so Bach; and so Rashi orot 3: they practiced in these countries not to eat on Pesach a dish of rice, millet, beans, lentils, sesame, and other kitniyot, even on the last Yom Tov; and so Chayei Adam general rule 127 orot 1: all dispersions of Ashkenazi exile practiced so, and also in Poland, for they too are considered among Ashkenazim, to forbid even to cook kitniyot and ritzkale and whole rice and millet — everything on account of error — see there; and see further below siman 464 in the gloss that mustard too — the Ashkenazi custom is not to eat it at all on Pesach — see there; and so Levush and Bach and other Acharonim.
levushei-serad/1:_: From A.C. and D.C., the rest of the oils are allowed to hang an epic instead of feeling that they will fall into the dish of forbidden grains and so on
levushei-serad/2:_: In order to nullify them — see Mishnah Berurah general rule 60 note 41.
levushei-serad/3:_: However there too they are accustomed to wash the wheat; and for matzah of the mitzvah in any case guarding from grinding is required, and grinding by a non-Jew does not help; and according to those who are lenient in siman 460 regarding a non-Jew's grinding, at least an Israelite must stand over him — see Kaf HaChayyim note 62.
levushei-serad/4:_: And we say in chapter Kol HaBasar — so it should read.
rabbi-akiva-eiger/1:_: That they use them all year — it is difficult to me: behold this is three noten taam: from barley to the mortar, from the mortar to oils, from oils to candles, and from there to oil — with this it is permitted, as above siman 452.
rabbi-akiva-eiger/2:_: It is called dough in dough and is not noten taam. If it was ground also with bran, one could say it does not mix well and one must shake the flour well that it mix well — then it is dough in dough. If the cap was heated in a chametz vessel — Beit Yosef — and mixed with another cap: one could say grinding does not help, for it does not mix well — we do not judge it as dough in dough; so too in Mishbetzot Zahav siman 467 note 8.
shaarei-teshuvah/1:_: Kitniyot — see in Mor u-Ketziah and She'elat Yaavetz part 2 siman 147 and in Kuntras Tov Ein of the Gaon HaAzulai zikhrono le-verachah at the end of Sefer Vaad LeChachamim: he wrote that in Ashkenaz and Poland, who accepted this stringency several hundred years ago, some great ones of Israel should not lighten for them, and one who is lenient breaches the fence etc.; and my uncle the Gaon zikhrono le-verachah in a responsum in manuscript wrote that the species called in our country pasulish is plainly a type of kitniyot, and he brought proofs from MaHarash on Mishnayot; and even where there is some duress, one should not permit them in these countries lest they come to breach the fence; and so the nation spoke; see in Lekut Maharil: after he brought the custom, 137, that one who eats them on Pesach transgresses the negative commandment "you shall not turn aside" and whoever transgresses words of the Sages is liable for death etc. — see there; and in one place some sages stood who wished to breach this and it did not succeed in their hand, because the sages of the generation, the great ones of Ashkenaz, were alarmed toward them and stood in the breach and upheld words of the Sages and decided the prohibition in these countries; and one should not learn from places that practice leniency from old and early times, before the decree of the great ones and their enactment spread among them — as regarding the ban on marrying two wives and the like; see in the aforementioned kuntras: a great one was stringent even in capers, although certainly it is fruit of a tree — it appears he wished to be stringent because the multitude did not know what it is and imagined it is also a type of kitniyot and would permit everything and breach the fence of the Rishonim; nevertheless even in places that accepted this stringency in capers, also if they were roasted before Pesach there is room to be lenient, as written in Shevut Yaakov part 2 siman 5 — and not like Chak Yosef, end quote; and in these places they plainly practice leniency in capers; and even so the zealous precede roasting capers before Pesach, and also examine before buying them to separate from them mixtures of rice and other species, to be clean from every concern of Pesach stringency; and may a good blessing come upon them; see in Shevut Yaakov there: he wrote in Taya that he heard many refrain because there is concern of deceit that they use taya and later return and dry them to sell, and perhaps they were first used with chametz; and so I heard from Shlomim; and so many — therefore one who guards his soul should distance from them, for on Pesach extra distance is required etc. — see there; nevertheless it appears one need not be concerned for vessels in which taya was cooked or if taya spilled into food; and some practice leniency in taya that comes from merchants in countries of its growth; and also experts testify it is kosher for Pesach by recognizing in appearance, taste, and smell that there is a difference between taya that was cooked and dried and taya that comes in the normal way of its growth and light did not rule over it in cooking at all.
shaarei-teshuvah/4:_: Permitted — see in responsum Chaim Sha'al part 2 siman 38: there is one species that looks like flour and is called in these cities saggi; it is made from tree moss of India and is permitted on Pesach; but in the city Londros they were clever to make like it from wheat flour and call it arineya di saggo; and Londros experts recognize it is made from this flour — I heard from a great scholar etc. — see there; and I wrote this so one should know to be careful, for sometimes physician-sages prescribe for one who has illness and pain to eat saggo, and one must be careful on Pesach that it is the one that comes from the Indian tree and not otherwise.
shaarei-teshuvah/5:_: Taste of fish. In the Book of the Book of the House of Ephraim, I extended these matters, and in the Book of Revelation, I wrote, “I have given them a short time, and from there the Talmud is here:
shaarei-teshuvah/7:_: To see the thick and thick, instead of Samuel C. N. N.C. in this case:
shaarei-teshuvah/8:_: Mitzvah — see in responsum Divrei Yosef siman 41: some practice that all matzah one eats on Pesach should be from wheat guarded from harvest; and in this there is neither yohara nor dispute nor lo titgodedu — see there; and they brought in Rabbenu Yerucham; see Peri Chadash siman 491 in customs of prohibition seif 1: those who practice eating matzah all Pesach from harvest — it is not called a fence but an extra matter that one does; and if he wishes to eat from matzah not guarded from harvest all days of Pesach except the first night, he needs release; and in Rabbenu Yerucham he brought in the name of Nachpeh Bekesef that release is required; and there he wrote: also one who practiced not to eat matzah but fruits the rest of Pesach days — although there is room to side not to release him, and so one who practices eating all matzah from harvest — nevertheless the essence is that release in regret suffices — see there; see YD siman 334; and the correct view: whoever wishes to practice separation in these stringencies or the like should stipulate explicitly that he does not accept upon himself to practice so always, only this time, for sometimes it happens he cannot act so and it comes to ruin; and if he forgot to stipulate, it appears release through regret suffices, as Machatzit HaShekel wrote in the name of my teacher zikhrono le-verachah; see in Tashbetz part 3 siman 117: wheat on Pesach may be ground in water-millstones — see there; and so they practice even those who eat all Pesach from harvest, for it is no better than matzah of the mitzvah; for although most are scrupulous that it be guarded from harvest, nevertheless they are not particular to grind in hand-millstones — only some practice rolling themselves also in this, and there is no yohara as stated; and so I heard they practice in Eretz Yisrael whoever can; see Peri Chadash: his view is that for matzah of the mitzvah on the first night one does not fulfill with guarding from harvest; and in Mishna Berurah siman 79 it was asked whether to be concerned for Peri Chadash's stringency here, and he answered: has he not seen the custom of Israel in all countries of Poland — none are concerned except the extremely scrupulous etc.; and for Rambam it is an asmakhta; and Rosh and many great ones are lenient; and in rabbinic [matters] we listen to leniency, end quote; and nowadays many consider themselves scrupulous and return to the granaries that there be wheat guarded from harvest at least to fulfill with matzah of the mitzvah; and so Machatzit HaShekel siman 460: in most famous communities they practiced matzah of the mitzvah from harvest; and in Eretz HaTzvi many practiced that all Pesach matzah be from harvest — see there regarding grinding by a non-Jew in hand-millstones one must be stringent — see there.
yad-ephraim/1:_: In R.C., D.C. and P.S., a reward rate should be eaten as a buffer in Pesaki and may be found to be a resident and a lawyer
